topics.title: Sequences
topics.text: So I was showing my dad cool ways to represent and solve sequences with geometry and pictures like $\frac{1}{3}+\frac{1}{3^2}+\frac{1}{3^3}+\frac{1}{3^4}...=\frac{1}{2}$. So I showed him $\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{2^2}+\frac{1}{2^3}+\frac{1}{2^4}...=1$. He didn't believe me I showed him geometrically but he said that there was always more space to fill. Basically he didn't believe that that sequence was equivalent to $1$. That got me wondering. If we have $\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{2^2}+\frac{1}{2^3}...\frac{1}{2^x}=\frac{2^x-1}{2^x}$. So that should mean that if $x$ is the infinite power, it's still always going to be a tiny bit less than $1$. It's weird....
